{{Short description|Prime number conjecture}}
In [[mathematics]], specifically in [[number theory]], '''Grimm's conjecture''' states that, for every set of consecutive [[composite number]]s, there is an equally sized set of [[prime number]]s, and a [[bijection]] that maps each composite in the former set to a prime in the latter set that it is divisible by. It was first proposed by Carl Albert Grimm in 1969.{{sfnp|Grimm|1969}}

Though still unproven, the conjecture has been verified for all <math>n<1.9\times 10^{10}</math>.{{sfnp|Laishram|Shorey|2006}}

== Formal statement ==

If <math>n+1,n+2,\dots,n+k</math> are all [[composite numbers]], then there is a sequence of distinct [[prime number]]s <math>\left(p_i\right)_{i=1}^k</math> such that <math>p_i</math> [[divisor|divides]] <math>n+i</math> for <math>1 \leq i \leq k</math>.

=== Weaker version ===

A weaker, though still unproven, version of this conjecture states that if there is no prime in the interval <math>[n+1, n+k]</math>, then
:<math>\prod_{1\,\leq \,x\,\leq \,k}(n+x)</math>
has at least <math>k</math> distinct [[prime divisor]]s.{{sfnp|Erdős|Selfridge|1971}}

== Consequences ==

If Grimm's conjecture is true, then
:<math>p_{i+1} - p_i \ll \Big(\frac{p_i}{\log p_i}\Big)^{1/2}</math>
for all consecutive primes <math>p_i</math> and <math>p_{i+1}</math>.{{sfnp|Erdős|Selfridge|1971}} This goes well beyond what the [[Riemann hypothesis]] would imply about [[prime gaps|gaps between prime numbers]]: the Riemann hypothesis only implies an upper bound of <math>O(\sqrt{p_i}(\log p_i))</math>.{{sfnp|Laishram|Murty|2012}}
